lead: A planar gate controls the channel only from above. Once the channel is very short, the drain competes with the gate and leakage climbs; thinner oxide and heavier doping help only a little and bring problems of their own. A FinFET stands the channel up as a thin vertical fin of silicon and wraps the gate over its top and both sides, so the gate controls the whole body again. Only a few universities teach this topic, but FinFETs have been the standard logic transistor since the 22 nm generation (2011).
prereq: You need: short-channel effects from MOSFET scaling and short-channel effects and the swing from Leakage and subthreshold conduction.

blocks.text: In a short planar device, field lines from the drain reach the source end of the channel through the body underneath, lowering the barrier (DIBL) and raising I<sub>off</sub>. A thinner oxide strengthens the gate but leaks by tunnelling; heavier doping shrinks the depletion regions but cuts mobility, raises junction capacitance and makes V<sub>T</sub> vary from device to device.

The better fix is a thin body. If the silicon under the gate is thinner than the depletion width, it is fully depleted, and the drain field lines end on the nearby gate instead of spreading through the body. The source barrier then barely moves with V<sub>DS</sub>: DIBL is small and SS stays close to 60 mV/decade. Control comes from geometry, not from a thinner oxide.

sections.h3: The fin and its effective width

blocks.text: The fin is a narrow ridge of silicon, of width W<sub>fin</sub> and height H<sub>fin</sub>, etched from the wafer. The gate dielectric and gate metal cover its top and both sides (a tri-gate); a double-gate FinFET uses only the two sides.

Because the body is so thin, it is left undoped or lightly doped. The threshold is then set mainly by the gate work function (the energy needed to free an electron from the gate metal) and by W<sub>fin</sub>, not by body doping. There is little body effect and less random variation from dopant atoms. W<sub>fin</sub> must stay well below the gate length to keep the body fully depleted, and tall, thin fins are hard to etch without bending.

sections.h3: Width quantisation and what comes next

blocks.text: A planar designer can draw any W. A FinFET designer chooses a whole number of fins in parallel, so drive strength comes in steps of one fin, and cells are laid out on a fixed fin pitch (the centre-to-centre spacing of the fins).

blocks.text: At the newest nodes the fin gives way to gate-all-around (GAA) nanosheets: horizontal sheets of silicon stacked vertically with the gate on all four sides, whose width can again be chosen.

examples.question: A tri-gate FinFET has W<sub>fin</sub> = 10 nm and H<sub>fin</sub> = 30 nm. (a) Find W<sub>eff</sub> per fin. (b) How many fins give at least 700 nm of width? (c) The process gives 1 mA per µm of effective width; find the current per fin and in total. (d) How many fins are needed for 720 nm?
steps: (c) 70 nm = 0.07 µm, so 0.07 × 1 mA = 70 µA per fin; 10 fins give 0.70 mA.
(d) 720/70 = 10.3, so 11 fins (770 nm): widths come in whole fins only.
examples.answer: W<sub>eff</sub> = 70 nm; 10 fins for 700 nm carrying 70 µA each, 0.7 mA in total; 11 fins for 720 nm.

traps: W<sub>eff</sub> counts the two sidewalls: using W<sub>fin</sub> alone undercounts the drive seven times here.
Fin counts are whole numbers; round up, never to a fraction.
FinFETs reduce short-channel effects; they do not remove them.

quiz.q: Define W<sub>fin</sub>, H<sub>fin</sub> and W<sub>eff</sub> for a tri-gate fin.
quiz.a: W<sub>fin</sub> is the fin width, H<sub>fin</sub> its height, and W<sub>eff</sub> = 2Hfin + W<sub>fin</sub> is the effective channel width of one fin.

quiz.q: Why does a thin, fully depleted body reduce DIBL?
quiz.a: The gate is close to every part of the body, so drain field lines end on the gate instead of reaching the source end through the body. The source barrier hardly moves with V<sub>DS</sub>.

quiz.q: W<sub>fin</sub> = 8 nm and H<sub>fin</sub> = 25 nm. Find W<sub>eff</sub> and the fins needed for 580 nm.
One fin carries 58 µA. How many fins give at least 0.6 mA?
Why is the threshold of a FinFET set by the gate work function rather than by body doping?
quiz.a: The fin is so thin that it is fully depleted with little or no doping, so there is almost no depletion charge term to adjust. The flat-band term, set by the work function of the gate metal, is what moves V<sub>T</sub>.

beyond: Gate-all-around nanosheets are in production at the newest nodes, and research is on forksheet and stacked complementary FETs that put the nMOS and pMOS on top of each other. Search for "GAA nanosheet" and "CFET" to follow the roadmap.

figure.caption: Cross-sections across the channel. The planar gate touches the channel on one surface, and the drain field can reach the body underneath. In the worked FinFET the gate wraps a 10 nm wide, 30 nm tall fin, so the channel runs along three faces: W<sub>eff</sub> = 70 nm per fin.
